items.title: Actress Evangeline Lilly Flees Hollywood: ‘God Has a Plan’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "So intense."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Actress Evangeline Lilly has had a sweeping Hollywood career, playing beloved characters in TV shows like “Lost” and films like “The Hobbit.”

But despite a wildly popular career, Lilly decided back in 2020 to step back from Hollywood — a decision that sparked quite a bit of media interest.

“It’s been six years now,” she said, noting the media caught on to the story after she posted a retrospective in 2024. “When I was 26, I was saying … all the things I wanted in my life … and I did it … I’m there,” she said. “I’ve already retired [by 2024 when the retrospective came out]. At that point, I’ve been retired for four years … it’s been a long time of adjusting.”

Lilly said she had no idea what the “consequences” of her decision might be, though she described moments of fear as she “let go of so much … power, influence, and potential money.” There was also the affirmation piece of the puzzle.

“When you’re successful at something, it feels really good when the world says, ‘We love you! You’re amazing!’ Like, this is a wonderful feeling,” Lilly said. “How do you walk away from that? And I’ve had moments of … gripping fear of like, ‘What am I doing?’ But, ultimately, the decision was one that was made in great conviction.

Before becoming an actress, Lilly studied political science and international relations and wanted to become a missionary, humanitarian, or diplomat.

“I wanted to make the world a better place,” she said. “And there are many people who will claim that actors are making the world a better place, that they’ve had an impact on their lives. But…I’ve always wanted a much more hands-on impact. I’ve done 22 years of hands-on humanitarian work in Rwanda.”

But Lilly said she wants to do more and wants to help people heal and find wholeness.

“I love telling stories, but I’d like to tell stories of my own instead of being in front of the camera,” she said. “I’d much prefer a quieter position. I’ve always hated being famous. I never made any secrets about that. I’ve always said being famous is the cost of the wealth that you can get as an actor. Like that’s what you pay for — the wealth.”

Now, she feels liberated and said she has stepped into a “total trust and surrender that God has a plan for my life.”

Despite mostly stepping out of Hollywood, Lilly is now lending her voice to a different type of project: “Legend of Destruction,” a film that tells the “story of the Jewish revolt against Rome, which ended with the destruction of the Temple in the year 70.”

“The film was originally made in Hebrew, and so I actually was able to see the fully completed piece before I came on board for the English version,” she told CBN News. “I didn’t understand what I was looking at. I didn’t understand what I was being invited into, but I watched the film, and within the first…three to four seconds of the film, I felt like I was just completely immersed in a way that most films don’t do for me anymore.”

What makes “Legend of Destruction” unique is that it’s made of still paintings, with Lilly, who portrays Queen Bernice, and other actors using their voices to dramatically retell the story.

“This story was so intense and beautifully told, and then also incredibly timely because it’s talking about a society divided unto itself,” Lilly said. “So a society that’s really broken and in civil strife and how that leads ultimately to mutual destruction amongst all of its people.”

Given that the film deals with the destruction of the Second Temple, many people will be interested in this unique film.

“At that time, Jerusalem was under threat from the Roman Empire. The Romans were coming to destroy the temple and to take over the city,” Lilly said. “The outcome of that could have potentially been different had the Israeli people been unified, but they were so disenchanted, they were so disenfranchised from one another, they were so divided that they were actually killing each other before the Romans ever even got a chance to arrive. It’s an incredible story. That’s what drew me in.”

The “Lost” star said the events in “Legend of Destruction” take place about 33 years after Christ’s death, meaning they are very much part of the world Jesus was born into.

items.title: Pastor Murdered by Colombian Gang Members He Was Evangelizing
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Heartbreaking.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A Colombian pastor has reportedly been fatally beaten by members of a criminal gang with whom he was actively sharing the Gospel.

The tragic killing took place in the city of Cartagena, where Jesús Alberto Puerta Pérez refused to allow the gangsters to use his motorcycle. According to a report from Christian Solidarity Worldwide (CSW), Puerta Pérez denied their request to use his bike one day after learning they intended to use it to move illegal drugs and that they had used it to commit crimes in the past.

Sources familiar with the situation told CSW, a U.K.-based Christian advocacy group, that the gang members were planning to entrap the preacher by unwittingly linking him to a crime through the use of the motorcycle. When he refused to participate on Oct. 7, the gangsters purportedly beat him to death.

So far, authorities have made no arrests.

Puerta Pérez, a married father of three, used his motorcycle taxi to make money and was a member of La Antorcha Encendida Church, an independent Christian congregation. The minister and his wife — both missionaries — regularly shared the Gospel with homeless people and gang members in Cartagena, in the Bolivar department of Colombia.

The couple had previously established a church in María La Baja, about 43.5 miles south of Cartagena, in the Montes de María area. But in December of last year, they fled to Cartagena after violent threats tied to Puerta Pérez’s preaching forced them to move.

Puerta Pérez leaves behind a wife and three children, ages 5, 6, and 12, as well as his wife’s elderly parents, for whom they have been caring.

Anna Lee Stangl, director of advocacy for CSW, urged Colombian authorities to conduct a “thorough and transparent investigation” into the preacher’s murder and to hold the gang members responsible for their alleged actions.

“CSW expresses heartfelt condolences to the widow and loved ones of Jesús Alberto Puerta Pérez, and we assure them of our sincere prayers and solidarity in this time of grieving,” said Stangl.

Last week, Scot Bower, chief executive of CSW, met with Gustavo Andrés Gómez Gaona, a foreign affairs counselor at Colombia’s embassy in London, and handed him a petition with more than 1,600 signatures, asking the Colombian government to restore protections specifically for religious leaders. According to CSW, Colombia removed protected status for at-risk groups from clergy in 2023.

Open Doors, an organization monitoring the persecution of Christians worldwide, ranks Colombia as No. 66 on its list of the 100 most dangerous places for believers around the globe.

“Whilst Christians from all denominations can face opposition for their faith in Colombia, those from Baptist and Pentecostal churches are particularly vulnerable to persecution from criminal groups,” the organization states. “Those who convert to Christianity – especially gang members and people from an indigenous background – can be especially at risk.”

items.title: Jess Connolly: The People Preaching Are Scared, Too
items.author: Jess Connolly
items.summary: I was standing on stage a few months ago, my hands gently trembling as I prepared to teach a room full of high-capacity leaders. I’d been invited to speak to C-suite executives and some of the most influential pastors in the country about fear, and I wanted to do it well. My message grew out…
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

I was standing on stage a few months ago, my hands gently trembling as I prepared to teach a room full of high-capacity leaders. I’d been invited to speak to C-suite executives and some of the most influential pastors in the country about fear, and I wanted to do it well.

My message grew out of years of coaching and research, and the work that led me to write You Can’t Be Brave Until You’re Scared. But its effectiveness relied on one variable: the people sitting in front of me would have to admit they were scared. These were people who didn’t often publicly acknowledge weakness.

I could tell early on that I didn’t have them. I heard fabric rustling and forks clinking against plates. I needed to help them see why processing fear mattered more than continuing to stuff it down. So I pulled out my metaphorical hammer and placed it on the table.

“How many of you have ever gone to the ER, certain you were having a heart attack, only to discover it was panic?”

Some giggled, unsure whether I was serious. I was incredibly serious. I’d heard versions of this story from so many high-capacity leaders.

“I’m serious,” I repeated. “How many of you? Maybe you didn’t make it all the way to the ER, but you seriously considered it?”

I wasn’t shaming them, and I think they knew it. I was asking because I cared.

The air went still. Nearly every hand in the room went up.

I’ve been leading in the local church in some capacity for two decades. When I say there’s a problem with how we’re handling fear, the call is coming from inside the house. I’ve been part of the problem, and I want to be part of the solution.

We’ve slapped platitudes and acronyms onto the hearts of terrified people while wrestling with anxiety ourselves. We’ve used fear to make poignant points in sermons, then shamed listeners for not having more trust. We’ve preached supernatural faith without explaining what it might look like to practice it. We’ve said God made our bodies good, but failed to compassionately shepherd people when those good bodies experience anxiety.

We need a better conversation about fear.

A few years ago, I began researching fear theologically, biblically, physiologically, and practically. I didn’t want to keep offering bumper-sticker phrases when we could ask better questions and find better answers. Four discoveries have changed the way I think about courage.

First, feeling fear is not a sin.

Fear is a natural, often involuntary response to a perceived threat. Before we’ve evaluated whether something is dangerous, our nervous systems may already be responding. Our hearts race, our hands tremble, and our bodies prepare to protect us.

Yet we’ve often treated these sensations as evidence of a spiritual problem, assuming that if we trusted God more, our bodies wouldn’t respond this way. But a racing heart is not a confession of unbelief. An anxious nervous system is not proof of failed faith.

What we believe about our fears and choose to do with them matters deeply. Experiencing fear, however, is not the same as choosing to be governed by it.

Second, the Bible’s commands about fear are invitations to trust, not weapons for shame.

Scripture repeatedly tells us not to fear and not to be anxious. We should take those words seriously, while paying attention to the people receiving them.

God tells Joshua not to fear as he prepares to lead people into an uncertain future. Angels tell terrified people not to fear. Jesus tells His disciples not to let their hearts be troubled, even as He prepares them for suffering. These words aren’t spoken because the circumstances are imaginary. They’re reminders of who God is in the middle of them.

And then there’s Jesus in Gethsemane.

The Gospels describe Him as deeply distressed and sorrowful as He approaches the cross. He doesn’t pretend the suffering ahead is insignificant. He names His anguish, brings it before His Father, and asks His friends to stay near Him in prayer. His distress is real, and so is His obedience.

We shouldn’t collapse biblical anguish into a modern clinical diagnosis. But Jesus shows us that profound distress and perfect faithfulness are not opposites.

Perhaps we’ve been so eager to teach people not to be afraid that we’ve forgotten to teach them what to do when they are.

Third, our obsession with fearlessness is hurting the people we lead and love.

We admire the fearless pastor, the confident executive, the Christian who always seems certain of the next step. But fearlessness isn’t the same as courage. And people who can’t acknowledge their fear may become especially vulnerable to being directed by it.

Unacknowledged fear can look like control, defensiveness, people-pleasing, or an inability to have difficult conversations. Sometimes the person who appears most confident is working hardest to avoid something they’re terrified might happen.

This isn’t just about pastors. We all influence someone, whether we’re raising children, serving a neighbor, leading a team, or showing up for a friend. Our fear doesn’t stay neatly contained inside us. It can shape the atmosphere around us.

We don’t need more fearless Christians. We need more Christians who know what to do when they’re afraid.

Fourth, paying attention to fear may be one of the most practical ways to practice courage.

Many of us have been taught to dismiss fear quickly. We quote a verse, remind ourselves that God is in control, and try to move on. Scripture is essential to our faith, but sometimes we’ve used true words to avoid honest conversations.

What if, instead of immediately silencing fear, we got curious about it?

What am I actually afraid will happen? What feels threatened? What am I believing about God, myself, or other people? And if the thing I’m afraid of happens, what would faithfulness look like then?

Naming fear doesn’t mean agreeing with everything it tells us. It means bringing it into the light, where we can examine it and respond thoughtfully.

Sometimes courage looks like taking the next step while our hands are trembling. Sometimes it looks like asking for help, seeking counseling or medical care, or admitting that the way we’ve been living is no longer sustainable.

Kingdom courage isn’t the absence of fear. It’s the willingness to move toward faithfulness in its presence, trusting God as we go.

Back on stage, as those leaders slowly lowered their hands, I knew I had their attention. I led them through a practical exercise: name the fear, consider the worst-case scenario, and decide what courage might look like moving forward.

It wasn’t all the work, but it was a start.

The change in the room was palpable. The mood felt lighter, the resistance was gone, and so was the pretense. I reminded them that fear didn’t disqualify them from leadership, but refusing to acknowledge it could deeply affect the people they were called to serve.

The same is true for you and me.

We are scared. There’s no getting around it. Pretending otherwise doesn’t just harm us. It shapes our churches, families, teams, and communities in ways we may not recognize.

I keep thinking about that room and all those raised hands. I wonder how many people there had spent years believing they were the only ones. I wonder how many people sitting in our churches believe the same thing.

Maybe the bravest thing we could do for the people around us is to stop pretending we’re not scared.

May the culture of modern-day followers of Jesus become more informed, more honest, more compassionate, and more courageous.

In Jesus’ name.

Jess Connolly is the author of You Can’t Be Brave Until You’re Scared (Baker Books), out now, as well as Tired of Being Tired and What Comes Next. She and her husband, Nick, planted Bright City Church in Charleston, South Carolina. She leads Go + Tell Gals and hosts The Jess Connolly Podcast. Find her at JessConnolly.com or on Instagram @JessAConnolly.

items.title: ‘Spare Us Yet’: Short Stories of Catholicism, COVID, and Cancellation
items.author: Jonathan Mittiga
items.summary:
Jonathan Mittiga

Faith sits quietly within each story, shaping how the characters confront their moral predicaments without necessarily resolving them.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Jonathan Mittiga

“Every society is a theocracy. Figure out what people have made into God, and their society snaps into focus.”

This line comes from Mr. Humberstone, a character in Lucas Smith’s 2025 short-story collection, Spare Us Yet and Other Stories (Wiseblood Books). Mr. Humberstone, a young academic and journalist, stands accused by an online mob of raping his ex-“girlfriend” (with girlfriend serving perhaps as too concrete a term; “They liked to keep it vague,” the narrator explains). 

In light of the controversy, Mr. Humberstone’s editor asks him to take leave from work, and he returns to his mother’s house, presumably to stew over the injustice he’s been dealt. In that way, the story offers a sort of behind-the-scenes of modern-day “cancel culture.” However, instead of actually fixating on the concept of “guilty until proven innocent,” Mr. Humberstone prays—for his ex-girlfriend, for her mother, and for the people accusing him. 

“He was pursuing a subjective state of well-being through the feeling of faith,” the narrator explains. “The important thing was to know that God was real no matter what he thought.” Yet he still reaches a human limit: “Knowing this did not make him feel better.”

This story, “Mr. Humberstone’s Trial,” finds the character at the end of a reluctant Christian conversion. “He passed what he thought was his excusable Marxist phase and his liberal humanist phase,” the narrator explains, only to find himself drawn, as if by an “irresistible force” to “eternal Christendom.” “Oh shit,” he thinks to himself. “I’m a Christian. Oh shit, oh shit, shit, shit, shit.” He writes a letter to his girlfriend explaining his conversion: “In a way, I can. In a way, I can’t.” Ultimately, words fail, and his endless reasoning is reduced to the virtue of faith.

Mr. Humberstone has changed his stance on premarital sex, for example, as a result of his conversion, and he expresses his wish to abstain—a desire that sits in stark contrast with the accusation against him. The “trial” mentioned in the title therefore refers not so much to a literal trial in court as to a trial of penitential suffering—the trial of a new Christian whose faith is being tested.

This is the strange moral territory Smith explores in Spare Us Yet. His characters are confused, compromised, and often wrong. They live in a world shaped by bureaucracies, online mobs, lockdowns, broken families, and political resentment. But, interestingly, Smith is not especially concerned with settling ideological arguments or telling us which side is right. He is more interested in how imperfect people reach for God.

On that score, the title Spare Us Yet recalls the Parce Domine of the Latin liturgy, “Spare, O Lord, spare thy people.” It is a plea to God to spare his people according to his mercy rather than punish them according to their offenses, and to deliver them in times of spiritual trial. These references do not exist within Smith’s stories simply to announce that the author is Catholic; Catholicism, for Smith, is not wallpaper. Instead, they provide windows into the interior lives of the characters, giving them a vocabulary for experiences that modern political language cannot adequately describe.

Likewise, the characters are not saints, and Catholicism is not a shallow evangelization device. Instead, faith sits quietly within each story, shaping how the characters confront their moral predicaments without necessarily resolving them. Each character reaches for it imperfectly in the search for truth.

In making sense of this dynamic, it’s helpful to think of the collection’s preface, “Prelude: Unit 1002,” as a frame for the stories that follow. In “Prelude: Unit 1002,” a nameless angel is called down with great fanfare to protect Christ’s altar. But this occurs in 1858, and the novel takes place during COVID. In the years that follow, the church is slowly abandoned—yet bureaucratic rules keep the angel from being released despite the abandonment, and he finds himself in the same storage unit into which the altar is placed. Eventually, he is released when the storage unit itself is abandoned and then sold to the highest bidder. Upon the sale, the altar is fed into a woodchipper, finally freeing the beleaguered angel from his earthly duties. Thus, the altar meets a darkly comic end. “Lord, have mercy on them!” the angel says as he ascends back to heaven. 

It is a strange and funny story but also a sad one—and it captures a paradox of the period Smith documents. Despite trending urban parishes and occasional sexy optics, the Church Militant—the living body of believers on earth fighting against sin, temptation, and the devil—has long been shrinking in cultural influence. Yet even as churches closed during COVID, Catholicism was acquiring a certain cultural cachet, particularly among young writers, artists, and intellectuals. Its institutional presence was appearing diminished at precisely the moment its aesthetics, traditions, and moral vocabulary were becoming newly fashionable. 

During the COVID lockdowns, this institutional decline became literal: Churches closed, public worship was restricted, and religious life was treated by governments as one more activity eligible for suspension—even as liquor stores remained open for business. COVID was topical when Smith’s stories were written, but, unfortunately, it remains relevant to understanding the current state of the church in larger culture today as well. 

Amid the lockdowns, the question of vaccination mandates in particular divided society: Should individuals be free to decline vaccination, or should governments be able to require it? This is another lens through which Smith investigates moral dilemmas. 

In “Lions Over the Bridge,” Smith follows a homeless man whose situation stems from his COVID-vaccine refusal. It would be easy to turn this character into a political martyr: an innocent man destroyed by an unjust system. But Smith refuses to make things that simple. The man is troubled in his own right. “HOMELESS DUE TO JAB,” he writes on a cardboard box as he begs on the street, even as he refuses his brother’s offer of a room. His suffering may be real, as may the forces acting against him, but this does not mean every decision he makes is reasonable. Yet he still reaches for truth, even using a quote he attributes to St. Isaac the Syrian: “Be like the bees and go where the good stuff is.” 

In his homeless, jobless wanderings, he casts judgement. He presses his diocese’s archbishop for forcing priests “to take the jab.” His mind is addled with diversions, and he pontificates, “You can’t pray ironically, and you can’t pray as if you are right. Prayer must always leave open the possibility you are wrong.” 

Smith’s characters are three-dimensional, and each of them—whether chasing after atheist graffiti artists, planning illicit Shrove Tuesday gatherings, or altar-serving at empty funeral Masses at the height of “stop the spread”—retains the possibility of an act of grace. Flannery O’Connor once described her own subject in fiction as “the action of grace in territory largely held by the devil.” Smith works in similar territory. His characters are never beyond the reach of mercy. And whereas O’Connor often ushers in grace through grotesque comedy, violence, or a sudden reversal, “Lions Over the Bridge” arrives at its own strange reversal. 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

The COVID years have been “memory-holed,” and when recalled, they are remembered differently by opposing political factions with conveniently alternative memories. Smith remembers something strange that he illustrates through his fiction: human beings trying to remain human while isolation, bureaucracy, and ideology reshape their society and their lives. 

Vitriol and pedantic moralization do not spew from these stories. There is no long anti-vaccine tract disguised as dialogue, nor are the characters merely puppets Smith uses to convert readers to Catholicism. Instead, Catholicism provides a language for sin, suffering, forgiveness, and grace without making any of those virtues easy. A challenging collection, Spare Us Yet rewards close rereading, with each story rich enough to warrant a review of its own. 

Still, complications linger. Even though much of its subject matter will resonate with those who lived through the COVID years, readers may not always know immediately what Smith wants them to make of a story. A few stories require a rereading before they can be fully absorbed. Individual lines can carry an unusual amount of weight, and, for better or worse, Smith often refuses to provide the moral conclusion that a less confident writer might underline at the end.

This density works better in some stories than in others. There were moments that demanded slightly more clarity. But the difficulty also seems inseparable from what Smith is doing. These are stories about people who cannot fully decipher the moral situations they themselves inhabit. Why should the reader be allowed to stand comfortably above them?

Spare Us Yet is not a demand that God punish our enemies. It is not even a confident declaration that “we were right.” It is a prayer uttered by people who know the world is disordered, who suspect that they are disordered too, and who can only beg for mercy over judgment. As we emerge from the COVID era and its consequences, Smith offers an important documentation of what occurred, the aftermath we’re still experiencing, the way Catholicism interplays with American life throughout the most unusual seasons, and the way art can still make us human after all.

items.title: Monday, October 19, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, today in our Gospel, Jesus tells of a rich man who has been so successful that he doesn’t have enough space to store his harvest.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Ephesians 2:1-10

You were dead through the trespasses and sins in which you once lived, following the course of this world, following the ruler of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work among those who are disobedient. All of us once lived among them in the passions of our flesh, following the desires of flesh and senses, and we were by nature children of wrath, like everyone else. But God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved— and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, so that in the ages to come he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God— not the result of works, so that no one may boast. For we are what he has made us, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand to be our way of life.

Psalm
Psalm 100:1b-2, 3, 4ab, 4c-5

Make a joyful noise to the Lord, all the earth.
     Worship the Lord with gladness;
    come into his presence with singing.
Know that the Lord is God.
    It is he that made us, and we are his;
    we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.
Enter his gates with thanksgiving,
    and his courts with praise.
    Give thanks to him, bless his name.
For the Lord is good;
    his steadfast love endures forever,
    and his faithfulness to all generations.

Gospel Reading
Luke 12:13-21

Someone in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the family inheritance with me.” But he said to him, “Friend, who set me to be a judge or arbitrator over you?” And he said to them, “Take care! Be on your guard against all kinds of greed; for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of possessions.” Then he told them a parable: “The land of a rich man produced abundantly. And he thought to himself, ‘What should I do, for I have no place to store my crops?’ Then he said, ‘I will do this: I will pull down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.’ But God said to him, ‘You fool! This very night your life is being demanded of you. And the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’ So it is with those who store up treasures for themselves but are not rich toward God.”

Reflection

Friends, today in our Gospel, Jesus tells of a rich man who has been so successful that he doesn’t have enough space to store his harvest. So he tears down his barns and builds bigger ones. But that very night, he dies—and all of it comes to naught. “Thus will it be for the one who stores up treasure for himself but is not rich in what matters to God.”

No matter how good, how beautiful a state of affairs is here below, it is destined to pass into nonbeing. That sunset that I enjoyed last night—that radiantly beautiful display—is now forever gone. It lasted only a while. That beautiful person—attractive, young, full of life, creative, joyful—will eventually age, get sick, break down, and die.

An image that always comes to mind when I think of these things is the gorgeous firework that bursts open like a giant flower and then, in the twinkling of an eye, is gone forever. Everything is haunted by nonbeing. Everything, finally, is a bubble.

But this is not meant to depress us; it is meant to redirect our attention precisely to the things that are “above,” to the eternity of God.
